652.title: Stand the night
652.hook: O you wrapped in garments, stand in the night, except a little (73:1–2)
652.howItsDone: Some Muslims pray tahajjud, voluntary night prayer in units of two rak'ahs, after sleeping and before dawn; some keep it nightly, others mostly in Ramadan or now and then, following the call of al-Muzzammil and the Prophet's practice.

segments.voice: Yesterday: masjid, the place where a forehead touches the ground. Your line was the mosque is his. Today a new surah, and a call that comes in the dark.

It's the middle of the night. The house is asleep. You're under a heavy blanket, pulled up to your chin, the warmest you've been all day. And someone speaks to you, gently, by the name of what you're doing. You, wrapped up. Get up. Not all night. Most of it, or half, or a little less. That is how surah seventy-three begins. It's addressed to the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ, and it calls him by his blanket: al-muzzammil, the one wrapped up.

Verses one and two, in Pickthall's translation: "O thou wrapped up in thy raiment! Keep vigil the night long, save a little." Verses three and four make it flexible: half the night, or a little less, or a little more. Some commentators hear the name as tender: not a formal title but a description, almost a nickname. They note that Arabs sometimes addressed someone by what they were doing at that moment, as a kind of affection. Some connect the wrapping to the beginning of revelation. Sahih al-Bukhari tells how, after the first revelation in the cave of Hira, the Prophet came home shaking and said to his wife Khadijah: wrap me, wrap me. Commentators differ on whether this surah came right after that, but it is counted among the early ones. Then the call: stand. Qiyam al-layl, standing the night in prayer. Verse six says why: rising by night is stronger for the heart and more fitting for words. The night is quieter. Nobody's watching. Your phone, ideally, is face down. Words said at two in the morning tend to be meant. Verse five gives another reason: We are about to send down on you a weighty word. Before the heavy work of carrying the message in daylight, the Prophet was given the training of the night. Today this is often called tahajjud, voluntary prayer after sleep, in the last part of the night. Some do it every night, some during Ramadan, some only now and then. The invitation is the same: get up from the blanket, and stand.

Sit as if it were the middle of the night: lower the lights if you can, let the house go quiet in your mind, and notice how your attention changes when nobody needs anything from you. If you pray, you might rise tonight or before dawn for two short units, two rak'ahs, even if it's only once this week.
Al-muzzammil. The one wrapped up: in 73:1–2 the Prophet, under his blanket, is called to rise and pray through the night, all but a little. Today's word.
Your line: stand in the night. The night comes first, then the heavy work of the day. See you tomorrow.

653.title: Measured tones
653.hook: recite the Qur'an in slow, measured rhythm (73:4)
653.howItsDone: Muslims who learn to recite the Qur'an study tartil and the rules of tajwid with a teacher: slow, clear, with lengthened vowels and pauses at verse ends, in prayer and in daily reading.

segments.voice: Yesterday: al-muzzammil, the one wrapped up, and your line, stand in the night. Today, how to recite once you're standing.

Play a podcast at double speed and you'll get the information. You won't get the person. The pauses, the breath before a hard sentence, the way a voice slows down when it means something: all gone. The same verse that calls the Prophet to stand the night tells him how to recite once he's standing. And the instruction uses one root twice, in a way that sounds like what it asks for.

Verse four ends, in Pickthall's translation: "and chant the Qur'an in measure." The Arabic is wa rattili al-Qur'ana tartila. Rattil, and then tartil: the verb and its noun together, which in Arabic adds emphasis. Recite it in measure, truly in measure. Tartil means a recitation that is slow, clear, evenly spaced, each letter given its full sound. How did the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ actually recite? His wife Umm Salamah was asked, and according to reports in Abu Dawud and at-Tirmidhi, she described his recitation as distinct, letter by letter, pausing at the end of each verse. And Anas ibn Malik, in Sahih al-Bukhari, said he would draw out the long vowels. From verses like this one grew an entire science, tajwid, the rules for pronouncing the Qur'an correctly: where to lengthen, where to pause, how each letter is formed. It is passed on from teacher to student. Different reciting styles developed too, slower and more melodic, or plainer, but they share the measure. Why does it matter? Verse five gives a hint: We are about to send down on you a weighty word. You don't carry something heavy at a run. You carry it slowly, with your full attention. Tartil is what attention sounds like out loud. The slowness isn't a delay before the meaning. It's how the meaning gets in.

Recite a short surah you know, al-Fatiha or al-Ikhlas, in Arabic or in translation, at half your usual speed, giving every word its full sound and pausing to breathe at the end of each verse. If you don't know one, say any line you love the same way, a word at a time, as if each word were heavy. Then sit in the quiet after.
Tartil. Slow, clear, measured recitation, each letter given its room. In 73:4: rattili al-Qur'ana tartila, recite it in measure. Today's word.
Your line: slowly, measured. Heavy things are carried at a walk, not a run. Day six hundred fifty-three, done.

654.title: Recite what is easy
654.hook: He knows you can't keep it all, so recite what is easy for you (73:20)
654.howItsDone: Night prayer (tahajjud) is held to be voluntary for the community; some Muslims keep a small, steady portion of it, or a daily portion of Qur'an recitation, following 73:20 and the hadith that the religion is easy.

segments.voice: Yesterday: tartil, slow and measured recitation, and your line, slowly, measured. Today, the last verse of al-Muzzammil, and it changes the rules.

Some resolutions are too big to keep. Run every morning. Read for an hour a day. Never check the phone after nine. Two weeks in, the whole plan collapses. Surah al-Muzzammil began with a huge ask: stand half the night in prayer, sometimes more. And the Prophet and some of those with him tried, night after night. Then the surah's last verse arrives, much longer than the others, and it says something that sounds almost like relief.

Verse twenty speaks straight to the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ: your Lord knows that you stand nearly two thirds of the night, or half, or a third, and so do some of those with you. He knows you can't keep count of it all, so He has turned to you in mercy. Then: recite of the Qur'an what is easy for you. And it names why. Some of you will be sick. Some will be traveling the land, seeking a living. Some will be fighting in the cause of Allah. The verse knows people's lives, illness, work trips, hard duties, and doesn't pretend they don't exist. A hadith in Sahih Muslim, from 'A'ishah, gives the history. When the surah began, she said, night prayer was made obligatory, and the Prophet and his companions kept it for a year. Allah held back the end of the surah for twelve months, then revealed this lightening, and the night prayer became voluntary. Notice what didn't change. The verse doesn't say forget it. It says recite what is easy. The practice stays; its size changes. And it adds the things that keep going no matter what: establish the prayer, give the zakat, lend Allah a good loan, ask His forgiveness. A hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari sits beside this verse: the religion is easy, and whoever makes it too hard will be overcome by it. The surah doesn't lower the bar to zero. It sets it where a real person can keep stepping over it.

segments.voice: Think of one good habit you dropped because it got too big: prayer, reading, exercise, calling someone you love. Shrink it until it's easy, one verse instead of a page, one minute instead of thirty, small enough that you'd be embarrassed not to do it. Then decide where it fits in your day.
Al-Muzzammil, the surah that began with a huge ask, half the night in prayer, before its last verse lightens it: recite what is easy. Today's word.
Your line: what is easy. Easy is not the same as nothing at all. Day six hundred fifty-four.

655.title: Arise and warn
655.hook: O you cloaked, arise, magnify your Lord, purify your garments (74:1–4)
655.howItsDone: Muslims pray in clean clothes on a clean place, and commentators read 74:4 as calling for purity of both garments and heart; the surah is remembered as the call that began the Prophet's public mission.

segments.voice: Yesterday: al-Muzzammil's last verse, and your line, what is easy. Today another surah begins with someone covered up, and a call to get up.

After the first revelation in the cave, the tradition says, the visits stopped for a while. Then one day, walking, the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ heard a voice and looked up. The same angel he'd seen in the cave was there, seated between sky and earth. He ran home shaking and said to his family: cover me, cover me. They wrapped him in a cloak. And under the cloak, the next words came. Surah seventy-four, al-Muddaththir, the one cloaked.

The surah opens, in Pickthall's translation: "O thou enveloped in thy cloak, Arise and warn! Thy Lord magnify, Thy raiment purify." The story of the cloak is in Sahih al-Bukhari, from Jabir ibn 'Abdullah. Jabir thought this surah was the very first revelation; others, following 'A'ishah's account of the cave, also in al-Bukhari, say al-'Alaq came first, and al-Muddaththir after the pause. Either way, these are the words that turned a private experience into a public mission. Four commands. Qum: arise, get out from under the cloak. Fa-andhir: and warn, tell people what's coming. Wa rabbaka fa-kabbir: and your Lord, magnify, the same root as Allahu akbar, God is greater. Before you warn anyone, set Allah above everything, including your own fear. And thiyabaka fa-tahhir: your garments, purify. Here the commentators split. Some read it literally: keep your clothes clean, especially for prayer. Others read garments as a picture of the self: purify your deeds, your heart, your intentions. Some hold that both meanings are meant, the outer and the inner together. Then verse five adds: and shun what is foul. Get up. Speak. Make Allah great in your eyes. Clean yourself, inside and out. It's a morning routine for someone about to face a hostile city. The Prophet had just said cover me. The answer was: arise. Not a rebuke. A job, and the dignity that comes with being given one.

Sit up straight and tend to what you're wearing: smooth a sleeve, straighten a collar, brush something off your knee, slowly, as if getting ready for something important. Then do the same inside, and notice one thing in your heart you'd like to wash out today, a grudge, a lie, a bad mood.
Al-Muddaththir. The one cloaked: in 74:1–4 the Prophet, wrapped under his cloak, is told to arise, warn, magnify his Lord, and purify his garments. Today's word.
Your line: arise. Under the cloak is not where the story ends. Day six hundred fifty-five, and counting.

656.title: Don't give to get more
656.hook: do not give expecting to get more (74:6)
656.howItsDone: Muslims are taught to give charity without reminding the recipient of it or expecting return, citing 74:6 and 2:264; many give secretly so that, as a hadith says, the left hand doesn't know what the right gave.

segments.voice: Yesterday: al-Muddaththir, and your line, arise. Two verses further on, a fifth command.

You know the gift with a string on it. The favor that comes back up in an argument six months later: after everything I did for you. The wedding present chosen to impress. The donation made mostly for the plaque. The help offered so that, one day, help will be owed. Most giving has a little ledger behind it, even when we don't admit it. Just after the call to arise, al-Muddaththir gives the Prophet a short instruction that goes straight at that ledger.

Verse six is four words in Arabic: wa la tamnun tastakthir. Don't give, seeking more. Tamnun comes from mann, which carries two ideas: to bestow a favor, and to remind someone of it, to hold it over them. Tastakthir means to seek more, or to count something as a lot. Commentators read the verse in more than one way. One early reading, reported from Ibn 'Abbas, is the plainest: don't give a gift so that you'll get a bigger one back. Another: don't consider what you've done as much; don't stand before your Lord counting your good deeds as if they were a favor to Him. A third: don't remind people of the good you've done for them. Many commentators say the verse holds all of these, the same habit seen from different sides: keeping score. The Qur'an returns to this in surah al-Baqarah: don't cancel your charity with reminders and hurt. A gift held over someone isn't really a gift anymore; it's a loan with interest. Then verse seven: for your Lord, be patient. The giving and the patience are a pair. If you give without expecting a return, you'll need patience, because sometimes nothing comes back: no thanks, no favor, no recognition. The verse doesn't promise you'll be repaid by people. It removes the repayment from the transaction entirely. You give, you let it go, and you wait, if you wait at all, on Someone else.

Think of someone you could give to today, time, a meal, a ride, a kind word, and check gently for a string: do I want thanks, credit, a favor later? If you find one, don't scold yourself; almost everyone does. Just notice it, picture cutting it, and picture giving without ever mentioning it.
Tamnun tastakthir. In 74:6, don't give seeking more: don't hold a favor over anyone, and don't count your good as much. Today's word.
Your line: give, don't count. A gift without a ledger is still a gift. See you tomorrow.

657.title: The self that blames itself
657.howItsDone: Some Muslims practice muhasabah, taking oneself to account, often at night, reviewing the day's words and deeds; teachers describe the self in three states drawn from the Qur'an: urging to wrong, self-blaming, and at peace.

segments.voice: Yesterday: tamnun tastakthir, giving without a ledger. Your line was give, don't count. Today a new surah, al-Qiyamah, and an oath by something inside you.

You said something sharp at dinner. Everyone moved on. But at eleven at night, brushing your teeth, a small voice starts up: that wasn't fair. You should apologize. Why did you say that? Nobody else heard it. Nobody else needed to. That voice, the one that won't let you off the hook, is ordinary enough to go unnoticed. The Qur'an notices it. At the start of surah seventy-five, it swears by it, right next to the Day of Resurrection.

Surah al-Qiyamah opens with two oaths. Verse one: I swear by the Day of Resurrection. Verse two, in Pickthall's translation: "Nay, I swear by the accusing soul (that this Scripture is true)." The Arabic is an-nafs al-lawwamah. Nafs is the self, the soul, the inner person. Lawwamah is an intensive form from lawm, blame: the self that blames, and keeps blaming, again and again. Why put it next to the Day of Resurrection? Commentators have suggested that the conscience is a small preview of that day: a reckoning that happens inside you, every evening, long before the final one. Muslim writers later drew a map of the self from three Qur'anic phrases. An-nafs al-ammarah, in surah Yusuf: the self that urges toward wrong. An-nafs al-lawwamah, here: the self that blames itself afterward. And an-nafs al-mutma'innah, in surah al-Fajr: the self at peace, called home to its Lord. Some teachers describe these as stages, or as three voices everyone hears at different times. Al-Hasan al-Basri, an early scholar of Basra, is reported to have said that a believer is always taking himself to account, while a careless person moves ahead without looking back. Notice what the blaming self is not. It isn't despair, and it isn't self-hatred. In the map, it's a good sign, a step up from the self that only urges: the part of you that still cares about the truth. The verse honors it with an oath. In that map, the aim is to listen to it, make things right, and move toward the peace after it.

Walk back through the last day and wait for the place where the small voice speaks up: that wasn't fair, that wasn't true, that wasn't kind. Don't argue with it, and don't pile on; just hear what it's actually saying, then ask it one question: what would make this right? Let the answer be small and doable.
Lawwamah: an intensive form from lawm, blame, the self that blames and keeps blaming, honored with an oath in 75:2. Today's word.
Your line: the voice that blames. Think of it as a friend with bad news, not an enemy. That's day six hundred fifty-seven.

658.title: Don't hurry your tongue
658.hook: don't move your tongue to hurry the revelation; its collecting is on Us (75:16–17)
658.howItsDone: One way Muslims learn the Qur'an is to listen to a teacher's recitation first and then repeat it, a method that echoes 75:16–19 and Ibn 'Abbas's account of how the Prophet received revelation.

segments.voice: Yesterday: lawwamah, and your line, the voice that blames. Today the same surah pauses on a moment inside revelation itself.

Ever tried to take notes while someone was talking too fast? You scribble, you whisper the words to yourself, you fall behind, and you lose the next sentence because you were still holding the last one. Now raise the stakes: the words are revelation, and losing even one is unthinkable. In surah al-Qiyamah, in the middle of verses about the Last Day, the Qur'an suddenly turns and speaks to the Prophet about exactly that: his lips, moving too fast.

Verses sixteen and seventeen, in Pickthall's translation: "Stir not thy tongue herewith to hasten it. Lo! upon Us (resteth) the putting together thereof and the reading thereof." The story behind it is in the first pages of Sahih al-Bukhari. Ibn 'Abbas explained that when revelation came, the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ found it heavy, and he would move his lips, repeating the words as they came, for fear of forgetting them. Then Ibn 'Abbas did something lovely: he moved his own lips, to show his student how the Prophet had done it. His student, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, did the same for the next generation, a gesture handed down like a family recipe. Then these verses came. Don't rush. Collecting it in your heart, and its recitation, are Our responsibility. Verse eighteen: when We recite it, follow its recitation. Verse nineteen: then its explanation is on Us too. After this, Ibn 'Abbas said, when Jibril came, the Prophet would listen, and when Jibril left, he would recite it as it had been recited to him. First listen. Then speak. The memory wasn't his burden to carry by force; it would be given. Surah Ta Ha has a similar line: don't be in haste with the Qur'an before its revelation is completed to you, and say, my Lord, increase me in knowledge. There's something here for anyone who learns anything. The fear of forgetting can make you grab so hard that you stop listening. The verse says: let go of the grabbing, and listen all the way to the end.
screen: `STIR NOT THY TONGUE TO HASTEN IT.`

segments.voice: Take a short surah, a prayer, or any line you love, and before saying it, listen to it in your mind all the way through, without moving your lips. Then recite it once, the way it came to you, and notice how it feels not to be chasing the words.
Jibril. In 75:16–17 the Prophet is told not to rush the revelation he hears from Jibril: first listen, then recite, since gathering it is Allah's to keep. Today's word.
Your line: don't hurry. A full week, from the night vigil to the listening ear. Day six hundred fifty-eight, done.

trapdoor: what you thought: speak slowly.
what it means: the Prophet was told to stop rushing the words of revelation; listening first, the memory would be given.
what a scholar hears: Bukhari's fifth hadith preserves Ibn 'Abbas moving his lips, shown to his student; 75:16–19 assigns gathering, recitation and explanation to Allah.
recall: arise, out from under the cloak

chat.says: Why was the Prophet told not to move his tongue quickly with the revelation?
options: Allah promised to gather it in his heart, so he could listen first, then recite.
Because reciting aloud was forbidden until the whole Qur'an was finished.
Because Jibril spoke too fast for anyone to follow, so it had to be repeated.
chat.meaning: 75:16–17: gathering it and its recitation are on Us. After this, the Prophet listened while Jibril recited, then recited it as it came.
